title: Everyday Muslim words
hook: Five short phrases, and you'll understand half of what you hear at the masjid.

screens.text: "Masha Allah, in sha Allah, alhamdulillah…" At the masjid it can sound like a code. It's really a handful of short phrases, and you already know some. Today you learn the rest.
**The greeting.** Muslims greet each other with ***as-salamu 'alaykum***, "peace be upon you." The reply is ***wa 'alaykum as-salam***, "and upon you be peace."
bubbles: Answering a greeting is a duty, and the Qur'an says to answer with one as good or better [Q 4:86].
Greeting people you know and people you don't is among the best deeds [Bukhari 12].

screens.meaning: Peace be upon you, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings
screens.when: The full greeting. Each part you add earns more reward [Abu Dawud 5195]. The short version, as-salamu 'alaykum, is fine any time.

screens.prompt: Someone greets you. What does the reply *wa 'alaykum as-salam* mean?
screens.feedback: It hands the peace right back. Returning a greeting is a duty [Q 4:86].

screens.title: Four everyday words: tap to flip

cards.back: **In the name of Allah.** Say it before eating or starting something [Bukhari 5376].
**All praise is for Allah.** For good news, when someone asks how you are, or after sneezing [Bukhari 6224].
**If Allah wills.** For plans about the future [Q 18:23–24].
**This is what Allah willed.** When you admire something good [Q 18:39].

screens.prompt: Match the moment to the word.

pairs.left: Your friend asks how your week was, and it was good
Your friend shows you a photo of her new baby
You see a sunset that stops you in your tracks

screens.situation: Chris walks into the masjid and a man he doesn't know says, "As-salamu 'alaykum!" Chris freezes. What's a good response?

options.feedback: Perfect. That's the reply, and it's a duty to return a greeting [Q 4:86].
Not quite. A greeting deserves a spoken reply. Even a nervous "wa 'alaykum as-salam" is great.
Friendly, and better than silence. Next time try "wa 'alaykum as-salam": he'll be glad to hear it.

screens.text: **A habit, not a test.** These words are a way of remembering Allah through the day, not a password. Saying "thank God" in English is praise too [Field Guide ch. 2].
bubbles: You don't have to fill your English with Arabic. Use the phrases when they feel natural; they'll come.
With non-Muslim family and coworkers, a normal "hi" and "thanks" is fine.

chips: Can I say salam to my non-Muslim friends?
What do I say when someone sneezes?

steps: Say Bismillah before every meal, and Alhamdulillah after
If you see a Muslim, greet them first with as-salamu 'alaykum
screens.optional_extra: Notice one moment today that deserves a Subhan Allah or a Masha Allah, and say it.

screens.text: As-salamu 'alaykum and its reply, plus Bismillah, Alhamdulillah, In sha Allah and Masha Allah: small words that keep Allah in your day.
Next time you hear the "code" at the masjid, you'll be speaking it.

prayerPhrase.when: Quietly. In the first rak'ah: opening du'a, then A'udhu…, then Bismillah…, then al-Fatiha. In every later rak'ah: just Bismillah… before al-Fatiha. [Q 16:98; Bukhari 6115; Q 1:1]

check.prompt: Someone says "As-salamu 'alaykum" to you. What's the reply?

options.feedback: Right. And returning a greeting is a duty [Q 4:86].
Not quite. That's for praising Allah. The reply to salam is "wa 'alaykum as-salam."

check.prompt: When do Muslims say "in sha Allah"?

options.text: When talking about plans for the future

options.feedback: Not quite. Before eating, say Bismillah. In sha Allah is for future plans.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Greeting: as-salamu 'alaykum; reply wa 'alaykum as-salam; returning a greeting is required and one may answer with better [Q 4:86]; greeting known and unknown people is a fine deed [Bukhari 12]; each added part brings more reward [Abu Dawud 5195, sahih per al-Albani].
- Bismillah before eating [Bukhari 5376]; alhamdulillah after sneezing, with the reply *yarhamuk Allah* and its answer [Bukhari 6224]; in sha Allah for future plans [Q 18:23–24]; masha Allah when admiring [Q 18:39].
- Ta'awwudh before reciting [Q 16:98]; wording *a'udhu billahi minash-shaytanir-rajim* [Bukhari 6115]. Hanafi: ta'awwudh once, in the first rak'ah (and when a latecomer starts making up); basmala quietly before al-Fatiha in every rak'ah; basmala isn't counted a verse of al-Fatiha [First Instructions on Worship ch. 7; Research Notes - Core Essentials and Madhab Map].
- These phrases are habits of remembrance, not requirements to belong; plain English is fine [Field Guide ch. 2; Welcome to Islam glossary].

**Likely questions**
- *"Can I say salam to non-Muslims?"* Scholars differ on starting the Islamic greeting with non-Muslims; a warm "hello" or "good morning" is always fine; if a non-Muslim says salam to you, reply kindly. Offer "Ask my imam" for more.
- *"What about sneezing?"* Say alhamdulillah; the listener says *yarhamuk Allah* (may Allah have mercy on you); you answer *yahdikumullah wa yuslih balakum* (may Allah guide you and set your affairs right) [Bukhari 6224].
- *"Isn't it weird to say these at work?"* Not required at all; use them when natural. In sha Allah in English is "God willing."
- *"Other phrases?"* JazakAllahu khayran (may Allah reward you with good: a thank-you), astaghfirullah (I ask Allah's forgiveness), Allahu akbar. Briefly.

**Escalate:** none specific.

**Don't**
- Don't make the convert feel less Muslim for not using Arabic.
- Don't call saying "Merry Christmas" or holiday greetings settled either way (Q5 territory; route to the imam).
madhabNote:
- **Basmala before al-Fatiha:** Hanafis and Hanbalis say it quietly and don't count it as a verse of al-Fatiha; Shafi'is count it as a verse and say it aloud in the prayers recited aloud; Malikis don't say it before al-Fatiha in obligatory prayers.
- **Ta'awwudh:** Hanafis say it once in the first rak'ah; some other schools repeat it in each rak'ah.
